key_terms.meaning: A system is BIBO stable if every bounded input produces a bounded output; for an LTI system this holds when all characteristic roots have Re(s) < 0.
For a closed-loop system, 1 + G(s)H(s) = 0; its roots are the closed-loop poles.
The region Re(s) < 0; poles strictly inside it give decaying exponentials.
A value of s at which the transfer-function denominator is zero.
A value of s at which the transfer-function numerator is zero.
A table built from the characteristic-polynomial coefficients whose first-column sign changes count right-half-plane roots.
Number of roots in the right half plane = number of sign changes down the first column of the Routh array.
Equation formed from the row above an all-zero row of the Routh array; its roots are symmetric about the origin.
Closed-loop poles nearest the jω axis; their terms decay slowest and dominate the transient response.
A measure of how far the closed-loop poles lie from the jω axis, linking pole location to damping and settling.
For a complex pole p, ζ = −Re(p)/|p|; it sets overshoot and decay rate.
Magnitude of a complex pole pair, ω_n = |p|; it sets the speed of oscillation.
The path traced by closed-loop poles as gain K varies from 0 to ∞ in 1 + KG(s)H(s) = 0.
The path followed by one closed-loop pole as K runs from 0 to ∞.
σ_a = (Σ open-loop poles − Σ open-loop zeros)/(n − m), where n = poles and m = zeros.
A point on the real axis where the root locus leaves or enters the real axis; found from dK/ds = 0.
Angle at which the locus leaves a complex pole: θ_d = 180° + Σ angles from zeros − Σ angles from other poles.
The gain K and frequency ω at which a closed-loop pole lies on the imaginary axis; found by Routh zero row or s = jω.

takeaways: For an LTI system, BIBO stability is decided entirely by the locations of the roots of the characteristic equation.
A root in the open left half plane decays with time; a root on the jω axis oscillates without decay; a root in the right half plane grows.
The Routh–Hurwitz test finds the number of right-half-plane roots by counting sign changes in the first column, without solving the polynomial.
Dominant poles are the slowest poles, so they decide settling time and overshoot more than distant fast poles.
The root locus shows how closed-loop poles move as gain changes, so it connects stability to transient shape.
Eight construction rules give the root-locus shape from open-loop poles and zeros, without solving the characteristic equation for every K.
A breakaway point occurs where two real-axis branches meet and leave the real axis; it satisfies dK/ds = 0.
The jω-axis crossing marks the gain at which a stable closed-loop system becomes marginal or unstable.
bank_note: Long answers usually combine a short statement of the stability condition with a worked Routh array, a sketched root locus and an interpretation of dominant-pole behaviour.

bank.q: State the BIBO stability condition for an LTI system and explain why every root of its characteristic equation must lie strictly in the open left half of the s-plane.
outline: Define bounded input and bounded output.
Write the characteristic equation and its roots.
Show that a root with positive real part gives a growing exponential term.
Show that a root on the jω axis gives a non-decaying term.
Conclude that strict left-half-plane roots are necessary and sufficient.

bank.q: Describe the Routh–Hurwitz criterion. How does the first column of the Routh array give the number of right-half-plane roots? Explain the special cases of a zero first element and an all-zero row.
outline: Build the Routh array from the characteristic polynomial.
State that sign changes in the first column equal right-half-plane roots.
Use epsilon for a zero first element.
Use the auxiliary equation for an all-zero row.
State the stability conclusion from the first column.

bank.q: Define dominant poles and relative stability. Explain how the real part and the damping ratio of a complex pole pair set settling time and overshoot.
outline: Define dominant poles as poles nearest the jω axis.
Relate real part to exponential decay rate.
Relate damping ratio ζ to overshoot.
Relate natural frequency ω_n to speed of response.
Explain why distant poles can be neglected in a first approximation.

bank.q: List the eight construction rules for a root-locus sketch and state the formula or condition used in each rule.
outline: Rule 1: number of branches equals number of closed-loop poles.
Rule 2: locus is symmetric about the real axis.
Rule 3: locus starts at open-loop poles and ends at open-loop zeros.
Rule 4: real-axis segments lie to the left of an odd number of poles and zeros.
Rule 5: asymptote angles and centroid.
Rule 6: breakaway points from dK/ds = 0.
Rule 7: jω-axis crossing from Routh array or s = jω.
Rule 8: departure and arrival angles from angle condition.

bank.q: For the characteristic polynomial s⁴ + 2s³ + 3s² + 4s + 5 = 0, construct the Routh array and find the number of right-half-plane roots.
outline: Write rows s⁴ to s⁰ with coefficients.
Compute the first-column entries.
Count sign changes.
State the number of right-half-plane roots.
Conclude whether the system is stable.

bank.q: Sketch the root locus for G(s)H(s) = K/[s(s + 2)(s + 4)]. Find the branches, asymptotes, breakaway point and jω-axis crossing.
outline: Place open-loop poles at 0, −2, −4.
Draw real-axis segments.
Compute asymptote angles and centroid.
Solve dK/ds = 0 for the valid breakaway point.
Use Routh or s = jω to find the jω crossing gain.

bank.q: For G(s)H(s) = K/[s(s² + 2s + 5)], find the angle of departure from the complex pole in the upper half plane and the asymptote centroid.
outline: Find open-loop poles at 0 and −1 ± j2.
Apply the angle condition at the complex pole.
Compute departure angle using angles from other poles and zeros.
Use σ_a = (Σ poles − Σ zeros)/(n − m).
State the asymptote angles.

bank.q: A unity-feedback system has G(s) = K/[s(s + 1)(s + 2)]. Use the Routh array to find the gain at marginal stability, then sketch the root locus and state the range of K for stability.
outline: Write the characteristic equation s³ + 3s² + 2s + K = 0.
Build the Routh array.
Set the s¹ row entry to zero for marginal stability.
Find the auxiliary equation and jω crossing frequency.
State 0 < K < K_marginal for stability.

bank.q: Use the Routh–Hurwitz criterion to find the range of K for which all roots of s³ + 3s² + 2s + K = 0 lie in the open left half plane.
outline: Write the Routh array with K in the first column.
Require every first-column entry to be positive.
Solve the resulting inequality.
State the open range of K.
Mention the marginal value at the boundary.

bank.q: Compare the Routh–Hurwitz criterion and the root-locus method for stability analysis. When is Routh sufficient, and when does root locus give more useful information?
outline: Routh gives only the number of right-half-plane roots.
Root locus shows pole movement as gain changes.
Routh is quick for fixed polynomial coefficients.
Root locus links stability to transient response and design.
Use both together when choosing gain and predicting overshoot.

bank.q: Explain the effect of adding a zero to the open-loop transfer function on the root locus and on the closed-loop dominant poles. Evaluate whether the zero always improves stability.
outline: A zero attracts branches of the locus.
It changes asymptote angles and centroid.
It can pull dominant poles left, improving damping.
It can also reduce relative stability if placed poorly.
Conclude that placement matters, not just presence.

bank.q: Two closed-loop pole pairs are −2 ± j3 and −0.5 ± j4. Which pair dominates the response? Estimate the settling time from the dominant pair and discuss relative stability.
outline: Compare real parts; the pair nearer the jω axis dominates.
Use settling time ≈ 4/|Re(p)| for a 2% band.
Compute for −0.5 ± j4.
Compare damping ratios.
Conclude which system is faster and which oscillates more.

bank.q: A plant G(s) = K/[s(s + 1)(s + 5)] is placed in unity feedback. Use Routh to find the marginal gain, then use root-locus rules to explain why the system becomes unstable and how a derivative zero may help.
outline: Write the characteristic equation.
Use Routh to find the marginal K.
Sketch branches and asymptotes.
Explain branches crossing the jω axis.
Show how a zero bends the locus left and improves stability.

bank.q: Distinguish BIBO stability from asymptotic stability for LTI systems. Explain the effect of a simple pole on the jω axis and of repeated jω-axis poles.
outline: Define both stability concepts.
State the pole-location condition for each.
A simple jω-axis pole gives a bounded oscillation but not asymptotic stability.
Repeated jω-axis poles give an unbounded term.
Conclude with the role of the characteristic equation.

glossary.def: Every bounded input produces a bounded output.
Every initial condition decays to zero as time tends to infinity.
The response is bounded but does not decay to zero.
The denominator polynomial of the closed-loop transfer function.
A root of the characteristic equation; a closed-loop pole.
A complex frequency at which the transfer function becomes infinite.
A complex frequency at which the transfer function becomes zero.
The complex plane used to plot poles and zeros of s = σ + jω.
The region of the s-plane where Re(s) < 0.
A coefficient table used to count right-half-plane roots without solving the polynomial.
The leftmost column of the Routh array whose sign changes give the number of right-half-plane roots.
An equation taken from the row above a zero row in the Routh array.
A closed-loop pole closest to the jω axis whose term decays slowest.
A measure of how far the closed-loop poles are from the jω axis.
A dimensionless number ζ that sets overshoot and decay for a second-order pair.
The undamped oscillation frequency ω_n of a second-order pair.
Time after which the response stays within a specified band around its final value.
The set of closed-loop pole locations as a gain K varies from 0 to ∞.
The path of one closed-loop pole on the root locus.
A straight-line path followed by root-locus branches at large gain.
A point where root-locus branches meet and leave the real axis.
The angle at which a root-locus branch leaves a complex pole.
The point where a root-locus branch crosses the imaginary axis, marking marginal stability.
